Every Conservative candidate in the next general election must sign a document committing their support to leaving the European Convention on Human Rights and scrapping the net zero target, Kemi Badenoch has confirmed.











The Tory leader said the so-called “candidate covenant” sets out “basic Conservative ideas based on our party’s principles”.




The two key policies prospective candidates must back are leaving the convention and dropping the target to reach net zero emissions by 2050.








Former Conservative MP and veterans minister Tobias Ellwood has already said the move bars him from standing for the party.




And the Liberal Democrats accused the Tory leader of forcing her candidates to sign a “Farage pact”.




Mrs Badenoch told the party’s regional East Midlands conference: “All Conservative candidates at the next election will be required to support the party’s official policy that Britain will leave the European Convention on Human Rights.




Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch says every candidate in the next general election must sign a document committing to leaving the European Convention on Human Rights and scrapping the net zero target.




“Let me be really clear: if any deal is signed with the European Union between now and then that prevents us from leaving the ECHR, we will reverse that deal too.”




Her stance on net zero has marked a significant shift in Tory policy since the party was in government and made the commitment.




She reiterated that Tories would need to back her plans to repeal the Climate Change Act of 2008 and the net zero target.













“It doesn’t matter if you are a member of my shadow cabinet, or someone who has been an MP for decades, or someone standing for our party for the first time – signing this covenant will be a mandatory condition to stand as a concerted candidate at the next election,” she said.




She insisted it is not a “purity test” and said while she hopes her parliamentary colleagues will sign, it is “entirely up to them”.







She added: “The Conservative Party has never been as united as it is now, and I would hate to lose any of my brilliant team.”




Former Tory whip Sir Mark Spencer took to the stage to become the first to sign the covenant, sitting at a table beside Mrs Badenoch and then posing with the documents in hand.

Play about 12-year-old ecojustice influencer wins Shakespeare’s Globe prize


Timothy X Atack wrote Tiny Alarms after workshops with children, who felt theirs would be the last generation of humans 




Tiny, a 12-year-old schoolgirl, is an ecojustice influencer, whose funny and disconcerting takes on the climate crisis go viral. She is also an alien, sent to warn humankind of its impending doom – but her mission is far more difficult than she anticipated.
This is the plot of Tiny Alarms, the first winner of Shakespeare’s Globe’s new climate playwriting prize. It was inspired by the real beliefs of schoolchildren for whom its author, Timothy X Atack, ran creative writing workshops exploring ideas around the far future.

“These young people, they were aged 11 to 15, roughly, and the whole group were pretty much united in the idea that theirs would be the last generation of humans. They were really matter of fact about it … in a way that kind of broke my heart and gave me immense fire at the same time,” said Atack.



When the Bristol-based writer, composer and sound designer saw the callout for the prize in February, he believed it was a “truly hopeful exercise”, and he knew this was the story he wanted to tell.
“As a sci-fi writer, I’m used to thinking on these big cosmic scales, and it felt like one of the best things I could do in relation to the climate crisis was to take this planetary threat that we have and weave it into a story that was essentially about parents and children,” he said, adding that as well as addressing “this deeply scary problem”, he also “wanted it to be funny”.
The judging panel, which included Lenny Henry, chose the play because they felt it most captured how it feels to be a young person navigating the climate crisis today.
“It’s the play I want my children to see,” said the prize’s chair, Nancy Medina, artistic director of the Bristol Old Vic. “The innovation, the humour, the journey that this story takes us on is one we all need to take in order to connect back again to our humanity and why we care.”

articles.jina_text:
Extreme global heat caused an unprecedented decline in the water levels of lakes, rivers and reservoirs around the world in 2023 and 2024, an international study has found.
The analysis of global water systems, a collaboration led by the Chinese Academy of Sciences, found that the planet’s surface freshwater fell sharply during the two years, which were the hottest on record. Global river flows fell to about 5.7% below normal, while the water stored in lakes and reservoirs dropped by 9.5%. Together, this was the largest synchronised decline in surface water since at least 1991.

As the planet warms, the water cycle becomes more extreme. A warmer atmosphere pulls more moisture out of soils, rivers and lakes, and hotter land speeds up evaporation even further. That moisture then falls as heavy rain elsewhere, often over oceans, causing sharper swings between drought and flood. This meant that during 2023-24, rivers ran low even in places hit by severe flooding.



To reach their findings, the researchers combined river flow measurements from 150 of the world’s major river basins with satellite data tracking more than 1.2m lakes and reservoirs between 1991 and 2025.
Dr Sulagna Mishra, one of the study’s authors, said: “The findings highlight an important paradox of climate change: a warmer atmosphere does not necessarily mean more water is available on land. Although global precipitation increased during this period, much of the additional rainfall occurred over the oceans, while many land regions experienced significant deficits.”
The effects were particularly pronounced in South America, where river flows dropped by 17.8% and water in lakes and reservoirs fell by 16.5%, even as some areas experienced extreme rainfall and flooding.
Dr Yi He, an associate professor in hydrology and climate change research at the University of East Anglia, said: “Parts of South America experienced severe flooding in 2023-24, yet the continent’s rivers carried much less water than usual over those two years. A river can flood during a downpour and still run low for much of the year.”
Water supplies around the world are facing multiple threats, including the super El Niño, droughts driven by the climate crisis, pollution and overexploitation.


The study’s findings showed how exposed the world’s water supplies were, the authors said. They said changes to fresh water were one of the main ways the climate crisis affected people and nature, and as the planet continued heating, it was becoming harder to predict how much water would be available.
Prof Christian Dunn, the chair of the British Ecological Society’s policy committee, said: “What’s particularly worrying about these findings is just how quickly our freshwater resources can decline, even in parts of the world we traditionally think of as being wet. And, as this study shows, just because we’re experiencing floods doesn’t mean we’re water secure.”

To avert the most catastrophic effects of warming, experts warn of the need for urgent and deep cuts to emissions, mainly from the use of coal, oil and gas. The world is already on track to blow past the goal laid out by the landmark Paris Agreement of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperature.
Yet, the Cop31 descended into disarray and disappointment after countries were unable to reach consensus on a deal that failed to mention fossil fuels. Nations rejected the agreement at a fraught closing session in Antalya on Sunday, almost two days after the summit was due to finish in what stretched to become the longest Cop in history.
The European Union, the UK and small island states such as Tuvalu refused to accept the text over the absence of references to fossil fuels, blasting the omissions as “greenwashing” and accusing oil states of “hijacking” the talks.
In the days covering the end of the conference and beyond, the world recorded six consecutive days with average temperatures 2C above pre-industrial levels for the first time ever. The daily global surface temperature reached 2.24C above the pre-industrial average on Monday, the highest ever, and was forecast to stay at similar levels for several days,. That reading beat the 2.12C recorded on 20 November, when delegates were still trying to thrash out a deal as Cop31 blew past its scheduled end time.
As I wrote in my analysis of the end of the conference, it is clear that we are at a crossroads, and change is needed:
“The failure in Antalya has brought the murky, Kafka-esque world of Cops right out into the open and exposed what has really been obvious to most outsiders. That this UN forum was intended to tackle the most critical threat of our time has not been working for a while. How can that not be the case, when after 31 editions we have yet to definitively turn the tide on emissions? Moreover, the role of the fossil fuel industry and its key national champions is now exposed for all to see. 
“Thanks to the success of Cop21 in Paris in 2015, the world has a framework through which the climate crisis can be addressed, in the form of the landmark Paris Agreement. Cop31 has undeniably illustrated Cops are not currently able to meet the demands of making that agreement a reality. Now the driving force should be what must be done differently to ensure Cop32 in Ethiopia next year can deliver the progress that Antalya failed to achieve.”

It’s time for Australia to tax our gas industry. It is a public policy no-brainer

Rod Sims


Fossil fuel companies are effectively not paying for the natural resource on which their businesses depend




Raising more tax revenue from our gas industry is the closest thing you will find to a public policy no-brainer. There are numerous calls for the government to return the budget to surplus quickly, in contrast to the current forecasts of continuing budget deficits well into the future. Those calling for a return to surplus generally want large net expenditure cuts, which are difficult given the pressure to spend more on an ageing population and on defence, just to name two areas.
I believe this will only succeed if, in addition to better control of expenditure, there is focus on the revenue side. In this context, by far the easiest step is to collect more tax from our gas industry.

Here’s why.
Tax revenue from the gas industry is well under 30% of revenue. All other major gas producers take more, usually a lot more. For example, Norway and the UK collect as tax about 75% of fossil fuel revenues, and still have strong production and a desire to invest. In addition, Norway takes equity positions in projects but the returns from this are not part of the 75%, which represents only the tax take.
Think of the revenue that is and has been forgone by successive Australian governments, and also the more than US$2tn sovereign wealth fund that Norway has steadily built up.
Australia’s gas industry does pay company tax but it pays close to nothing for the gas that belongs to all Australians.
Let’s understand this. If you start a business in Australia by building a factory or providing services you need to pay only company tax. But if you build a business by getting access to a scarce natural resource that belongs to all Australians, you need to also pay for that. This is what happens all around the world, sometimes by paying royalties or, better, taxes that seek a fair share of the benefits from obtaining the resource.

However, the exact amount you pay will depend on your tariff, the size of your home and how much energy you use.

The price cap, set by Ofgem, limits how much suppliers can charge for each unit of gas and electricity on variable tariffs.



It is not a cap on your total bill, so the more energy you use, the more you pay.



From January, the cap on the gas unit rate rises from 7.97p to 10.96p per kilowatt hour (kWh), up 37.5 per cent, while electricity rises from 26.32p to 32.69p, up 24 per cent.

The price cap, set by Ofgem, limits how much suppliers can charge for each unit of gas and electricity on variable tariffs. 
It is not a cap on your total bill, so the more energy you use, the more you pay. 
From January, the cap on the gas unit rate rises from 7.97p to 10.96p per kilowatt hour (kWh), up 37.5 per cent, while electricity rises from 26.32p to 32.69p, up 24 per cent.



 
Bills also include a standing charge – a fixed daily fee, which the cap also limits, covering costs such as keeping homes connected to the energy network. 
Standing charges are barely changing, so almost all of the rise comes through unit rates. 
For a household with typical energy use paying by Direct Debit, Ofgem says the new cap is equivalent to £2,166 a year – up £443 from £1,723. 
The new cap lasts until 31 March. Ofgem is expected to announce prices for April to June around 23 February. 
Cornwall Insight, an energy consultancy that forecasts where the price cap is heading, expects only a small fall in April. Its first forecast points to a drop of 1 per cent, leaving a typical bill at £2,151 a year. 
Its retail markets principal Craig Lowrey said the expected fall was “so small that many households will barely notice it”. 
How much more you will pay 

 
  
Analysis by The i Paper has identified how much homes of different sizes will pay, using government figures on how much gas and electricity a typical home of each size uses in England and Wales.



 
The figures are for a typical home of each size paying by Direct Debit – actual bills will be higher or lower depending on how much energy a household uses. 
A typical one-bedroom home will pay £1,424 a year, up from £1,163. That is an extra £262, or around £22 a month. 
A typical three-bedroom home – the most common size – will pay £2,332, up from £1,848. That is an extra £484 a year or £40 a month. A four-bedroom home faces an annual rise of £627 – that is an additional £52 per month. 
The biggest rise is for homes with five or more bedrooms. Their bill goes from £3,055 to £3,925 – an extra £870 a year, or around £72 a month. 
Bigger homes are hit hardest because they use more energy, and it is unit rates that are rising. 
Across homes of all sizes, the typical rise is £461 – a little above Ofgem’s £443, as Ofgem’s benchmark assumes slightly lower energy use.

Most modern boilers have a filling loop, usually a flexible silver hose with valves at either end, which allows you to let water back into the heating system following your manufacturer’s instructions. If in doubt, an engineer can do it for you. When it comes to anything that involves gas though, a gas-safe engineer should be called out to look at the problem. 
Not getting an annual service 
Annual servicing is one of the most important steps you can take to keep the boiler working safely and efficiently but according to research by Which?, four in 10 homeowners with an older heating system were not having it serviced annually, with over a quarter of them taking a “wait until it breaks” approach. Based on their research last year, a typical service costs between £70 and £110. 
Turner says “you should have a boiler service yearly at the absolute minimum” to ensure it’s working correctly and reduce the risk of carbon monoxide build-up.

articles.jina_text:
For the first time, the world has experienced six consecutive days of temperatures 2C warmer than preindustrial levels, the Guardian has learned.
This record hot streak, which is continuing, is too brief to signify that the upper range of the Paris climate agreement target has been breached, but scientists said it was an early indication of what is to come unless fossil fuel emissions are rapidly eliminated. It is also likely to feed into growing scientific concerns that global heating may be accelerating.

The daily global surface temperature rose to its highest ever point above preindustrial levels, 2.24C, on Monday, the most recent day for which data is available, and is forecast to persist at similarly high levels for at least several more days.

“This is an exceptional global temperature anomaly,” said Samantha Burgess, the strategic lead for climate at the Copernicus Climate Change Service. “We have seen record global temperatures persist for several months now. While individual days fluctuate, temperatures at this level are a striking indication of how much the climate has heated.”


There have only been two other periods when daily temperatures climbed over 2C, in November 2023 and February 2024, but they did not last as long or climb as high as this latest spell.
“Another day, another global temperature record,” said Zeke Hausfather, a climate researcher at Berkeley Earth, , adding that the previous record of 2.05C over the 1850-1900 baseline, set in 2023, has been “smashed”.
The temperature spikes are driven by long-term global heating caused by humans burning fossil fuels, and by an unusually large El Niño, which is approaching its peak.

The last El Niño on this scale was in the 1870s, when it led to a mass famine that killed 50 million people, Burgess said. Scientists expect the current El Niño to peak between now and January, though its full impact will not be felt until several months afterwards.


The extra heat in the global system is already creating feedbacks that worsen the climate crisis, such as drought and fire in the tropical rainforests of Indonesia and in the Amazon.
The UK Met Office predicts a very large rise in atmospheric CO2 in the coming months, largely because tropical ecosystems are growing less vigorously due to droughts, which diminishes their capacity to remove carbon from the atmosphere.
“This will amplify the buildup of CO2 in the atmosphere driven by fossil fuel burning,” said Richard Betts, the head of climate impacts research at the Met Office Hadley Centre. “The CO2 increase from this year to next will be about 3.5 parts per million, a third faster than in recent years and nearly twice as fast as what it should have been limited to if we’d been on track to limit global warming to 1.5C.”

I only had an old iPhone, was a long way back, and remember thinking: “I’d love a long lens to see the expression on their faces.”

It’s about the natural geometry and negative space in the frame.
It’s tragedy and resignation. On reflection my Christmas jumper analogy probably wasn’t the best. It’s planet-defining stuff, all of this. Sorry, what? Negative space?


That’s the area above his head with nothing in it. It’s shaped like a V and it’s drawing your eyes down to this amazing expression that I’ve actually seen Bowen make before. He does it occasionally.
So it might just be a lucky shot?

This tiny Asian flying frog – with some rather unusual egg-laying habits – has been discovered in Sulawesi, an island near Borneo, Indonesia. 
Scientists from Bogor Zoology Museum, a laboratory in Bogor, and the University of California, Davis, discovered the new species. 
Sitting on the equator, Sulawesi is among the most ancient spots on Earth, home to rainforests lit up by bioluminescent mushrooms and a volcano. 

 
From 2009 to 2013, researchers waded through rivers and camped out during lightning storms to survey the mountainous regions’ wildlife. 
 
   
The frog is a newly discovered species (Picture: UC Davis MWFB Archives, NIH-ICBG Expeditions) 
 
 Sign up for all of the latest stories  
 
Start your day informed with Metro's News Updates newsletter or get Breaking News alerts the moment it happens.  
    
According to their paper in the journal Zootaxa, it was in the seasonal mountain lake Danau Coca-Cola that they saw Rhacophorus kurniatiae. 

 
The thousands of frogs live more than 6,100 feet above sea level, sporting pointed snouts and giant webbed feet used to glide from tree to tree. 
‘You don’t really see frogs in big congregations like that. This was something super special,’ said co-author Alan Hitch, a research affiliate with the UC Davis Museum of Wildlife and Fish Biology. 
‘Rhacophorus’ is what scientists call flying frogs – but how these critters lay eggs is different from other shrub amphibians.  
They give birth using a ‘gelatinous matrix’, said co-author Alamsyah Elang Nusa Herlambang, a researcher with Museum Zoologicum Bogoriense.  
In simple terms, rather than foamy nests in water, the frogs lay eggs in a blob of clear jelly that dangles off a leaf, looking over the remote lake. 
 
   
Frogspawn grow up in the gel sacks (Picture: UC Davis MWFB Archives, NIH-ICBG Expeditions) 
After a few weeks, squint at these gooey bubbles and you’ll see tadpoles wriggling inside. 
‘It’s unique,’ added Herlambang. 
To check if the frogs weren’t one of the other 40 Rhacophorus out there, the team examined 28 of its physical traits, its DNA and its ribbiting. 
Andrew Engilis Jr., curator of the UC Davis Museum of Wildlife and Fish Biology, said the Rhacophorus kurniatiae is a ‘cryptic species’. 
In other words, while they look and jump like most flying frogs, they’re genetically distinct enough to be considered separate species. 
After realising they had stumbled on a new species, Indonesian scientists named it after the late Hellen Kurniati, an herpetologist, an expert in frogs. 
 
   
The species can fly using its webbed feet (Picture: UC Davis MWFB Archives, NIH-ICBG Expeditions) 
 
   
They call a pond in Indonesia’s Mekongga Mountains home (Picture: UC Davis MWFB Archives, NIH-ICBG Expeditions) 
‘She had a heart of gold,’ Hitch said, ‘and I think that’s part of what drove her to do such great work.’ 

 
Most creatures on Sulawesi are endemic, meaning they’re found nowhere else on Earth.

The UK has criticised the “immensely disappointing” failure to reach agreement at the United Nations Cop31 climate summit, formally objecting to a proposed deal that “moves us backwards on the science” of tackling climate change.

EU, UK and some of developing world object to main text that ‘failed to meet the moment’ and did not mention fossil fuels 
 Cop31 live blog: longest climate summit ever faces collapse




The EU, the UK and allies in the developing world rejected what they called an unacceptable deal on the future of the climate, which failed even to mention fossil fuels, in a dramatic finish to the Cop31 UN talks in Turkey.
The proposed deal “failed to meet the moment”, said Ireland’s environment minister, Darragh O’Brien, speaking for the EU. “We will not endorse a decision that does not respond to the science and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required. [It] does not even mention fossil fuels.”

As the talks, scheduled to end on Friday, dragged on into Sunday afternoon it was clear that the “Antalya pact”, drafted by the Turkish and Australian joint presidencies of the summit, would not achieve the consensus needed to pass.


The Antalya pact invites countries to electrify their economies, calls for rich countries to provide finance to the poor to help them adapt to the impacts of the climate crisis, and calls on countries to minimise the “overshoot” of the 1.5C global heating threshold, of the Paris agreement.
But it failed to endorse the “transition away from fossil fuels” that more than 130 countries demanded, and included controversial provisions on “carbon capture and storage” (CCS) technology that campaigners have said perpetuates fossil fuels.
The presidencies avoided outright collapse of the “conference of the parties” by passing decisions on various related matters, including the “just transition” to help workers in high-carbon industries shift to a low-carbon economy.
But Murat Kurum, Turkey’s Cop president, acknowledged there was no agreement on the draft “cover decision” text and so it had not been adopted.
“We have done our utmost; ultimately, we have not imposed this text on anyone, nor have we issued an ultimatum ⁠such as a ‘take it or leave it’ demand,” he said. “It is clear that there are parties in this hall who oppose this text. We recognise ⁠that there is no consensus on this document. Therefore, these decisions have not been adopted.”


Many countries, including the EU, UK and many developing countries including small island states and some of the poorest countries, said they could not support the Antalya pact deal, which was supposed to be the “cover decision”, or main outcome, of the Cop.
In a dramatic intervention, O’Brien said on behalf of the EU that it could not accept the final text in its current form. “It fails to meet the moment … We will not endorse a cover decision or an Antalya pact that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change.” He said the EU would not accept a decision “that greenwashes fossil fuels”.

Efforts to avert the collapse of talks at the UN COP31 summit have faced further delays on the second day of overtime, as countries struggle to reach a new global climate deal.
A new draft agreement was published in the early hours of Sunday which the Turkey and Australia co-hosts hoped would bridge the divide between nations.
Although it still includes no specific reference to "transitioning away from fossil fuels" - an omission in the previous draft that sparked threats of walkouts - it does acknowledge a previous commitment made by countries to do just that three years ago.
Countries were expected to reconvene to decide whether to approve a new deal, but that meeting was delayed on Sunday morning.
The president of the talks, Turkey's Environment Minister Murat Kurum, told the BBC he was "hopeful" of a breakthrough as he entered the summit on Sunday. 
"We will be happy soon enough," he said. 
But that outlook was not shared by the EU, which the BBC understands considers the new text to be a backward step. 
The EU and Pacific states had been arguing against the removal of fossil fuels from the draft text. The EU has not yet reacted to this latest draft.
The Africa Group is likely to be disappointed at this latest iteration as it includes no specific figure on money for adaptation and instead kicks that decision to future meetings.
The new draft also includes for the first time a recognition that the world is on track to miss the crucial goal of keeping temperatures below 1.5C of warming.
These talks are approaching the longest-running in the COP history. 
If countries cannot reach consensus - as required by the UN's climate talks process - the negotiations could be suspended until next year. This has only happened once before since countries started holding COP climate meetings in 1995.
Just hours before the new text was published, EU Commissioner for Climate Wopke Hoekstra said if the bloc could not get "what is needed in terms of climate action... then there's no deal."
Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, the UK's chief negotiator, struck a more hopeful tone, saying her team was still working to get an agreement.
A draft deal unveiled earlier this week called for a faster phase-out of fossil fuels, but a second, pared-down version released on Thursday stripped away all mentions of coal, oil and gas - sparking threats of a walk out.
The fallout led to the summit in Antalya blowing past the original deadline of Friday. On Saturday negotiating teams who had Sunday morning flights were rescheduling them - a sign a deal was still not in sight, and raising the risk that as teams eventually had to leave, the meeting could lose the critical numbers needed to pass an agreement.
As part of a last ditch effort to produce an acceptable text, the European Union and Saudi Arabia - who were deeply divided over the future of fossil fuels - were brought together on Saturday to seek a compromise.

Negotiations at the COP31 UN climate summit in Turkey are in deadlock, having run through the night, as countries remain unable to agree on a new global climate deal.
In a late intervention on Friday, a group of countries led by France and Panama pushed back against the draft agreement which included no reference to reducing the world's demand for fossil fuels. 
Separately, the Africa Group are fighting to get commitments on more money for adaptation, saying they did not come to the COP "to beg".
A new and potentially final agreement is expected to be published on Saturday.

Ministers from island states, Panama, and a strong contingent of EU nations which include Spain, France, Belgium, Sweden and Finland have said they are pushing to get a commitment to move away from oil, gas and coal back into the final agreement after fossil fuel producers led by Saudi pushed for its removal.

She took aim at several references in the text to carbon capture, use and storage - the technology that takes emissions when they are released and stores them underground - as a licence for other countries to keep burning oil and gas.

China commits to low-carbon electrification and help for others to improve


Exclusive: Countries at Cop31 are being urged to commit to deriving 35% of their energy from electricity by 2035 
 
 
Cop31 live – latest updates  




China is pushing for rapid electrification of its economy using low-carbon energy and will help other countries do the same, a senior member of the Chinese delegation at the Cop31 UN climate summit has said.
Wang Yi, a professor of energy and environment policy at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and a senior adviser to China’s government, said: “End-use electrification is a very clear direction. We can follow this direction while making the source of electricity clean. That’s the way to go forward.”

China is the biggest emitter of greenhouse gases by far, producing more than a quarter of the world’s total, so its push for electrification is significant.
At Cop31, countries are being asked to sign up to a target of deriving 35% of final energy consumption from electricity by 2035. Australia, the president of the negotiations, and the host nation Turkey have pushed the target and on Friday night Australia and China signed a joint statement endorsing the “35:35” goal.


But in the second draft text of the probable outcome from Cop31, released on Thursday, the electrification pledge was downgraded to one of a suite of voluntary options countries can take up to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions.
In an interview with the Guardian at the talks, Wang said: “China will do our best to realise clean end-use electrification, and also help other countries to improve. China has significantly reduced the cost of clean technology and products and we would like to share our experience with other countries.”
Experts have said electrification is the next vital step in the shift to a low-carbon economy, as the only way to diminish the close to 80% of fossil fuels still used for primary energy, mostly for transport, heating and industry.
While civil society organisations want any commitment made on electrification to specify that it must be met from clean sources, a pledge that leaves the choice to countries is likely to have more widespread support, as many – including China and India – are resistant to anything they feel smacks of “top down” interference in national plans.
But campaigners argue that allowing individual countries to decide risks leaving the door open to more gas-fired power plants. Some compromise language is also possible that would urge countries to decarbonise their power.

articles.title: Plans unveiled for one of UK's biggest solar farms
articles.raw_rss: Low Carbon wants to install solar panels across 4,200 acres (1,700 hectares) of Essex countryside.
articles.raw_meta: Low Carbon wants to install solar panels across 4,200 acres (1,700 hectares) of Essex countryside.
articles.jina_text:
Plans have been unveiled to build one of the biggest solar farms in the UK across a huge slice of Essex's Dengie Peninsula.
Low Carbon wants to install panels across 4,200 acres (1,700 hectares) of sprawling countryside between Burnham-on-Crouch and Bradwell-on-Sea.
The developer said the site could generate 1GW of power - enough to supply 250,000 homes, or every house between Basildon and Shoeburyness.
However, critics have questioned how the project will impact wildlife and local roads during construction.
The scheme has been deemed a nationally significant infrastructure project, which means the government has the final say on whether it will go ahead.
Simon Morgan, the Conservative leader of Maldon District Council, said it had emerged "out of the blue".
"It was a complete shock when we saw the extent of the area that's being planned," he told the BBC.
"It's almost, in my view, one-third of the land in the Dengie Peninsula, which is quite an extensive amount of land to be put under solar panels."




Image source, Jamie Niblock/BBC
Image caption, 

The land proposed for development is equivalent to about 2,400 football pitches




Plans published online by Low Carbon showed seven potential sites have been earmarked for solar farms and battery energy storage systems.
They stretch from near the decommissioned Bradwell nuclear power station to Burnham-on-Crouch, passing Tillingham and Southminster.
In total, the land proposed for development is equivalent to about 2,400 football pitches. Low Carbon described it as one of the biggest solar farms in the UK.
"The scale of this has slightly knocked people sideways," said James Taylor, chairman of the Dengie Climate Action Partnership.




Image source, Jamie Niblock/BBC
Image caption, 

James Taylor is torn on how he feels about the plans




Taylor is torn between championing renewable energy and feeling concerned about how the site could impact wildlife, particularly as it is a crucial migration route for birds.
"It's an enormously important international area for wildlife and a Site of Special Scientific Interest," added Roger Morland, the chairman of Burnham Against Non-Sustainable Development.
Low Carbon is aiming to consult residents on its plan by summer 2027 and then submit it to the Planning Inspectorate by the end of that year.

African ministers say they ‘didn’t come here to beg’, with civil society groups calling it the ‘worst Cop ever’




Crucial climate talks headed into overtime on the last official day of the Cop31 UN summit as countries continued to argue over a draft deal that was silent on fossil fuels, with a host of other contentious issues complicating negotiations.
Nearly 200 countries struggled to bridge their differences after two weeks of intense talks and impassioned speeches in Antalya, Turkey, about the effects of climate breakdown around the world, with a scheduled finish of Friday evening breached.

“At this point, no one is happy,” Brazil’s national secretary for climate change, Aloisio Lopes Pereira de Melo, told reporters.
The Guardian understands there will probably not be a new draft of an agreement for negotiators to pore over until Saturday morning. A sprawling initial draft deal released earlier this week included strong calls to accelerate the phase-out of coal, oil and gas, but a second, shorter version on Thursday did not include mention of fossil fuels and weakened goals on electrification.
On Friday there was a dramatic intervention by African ministers early on in the day, with one saying: “We didn’t come here to beg.” Civil society groups, who have a mandated role at the talks, declared it the “worst Cop ever”, with none of their priorities making it through the negotiations. They were particularly frustrated by a failure to take forward a just transition mechanism agreed last year, which they hoped would embed social, racial and economic justice into a low-carbon future.

But although agreements are made on food, carbon emissions and youth mobility there remains a sticking point over whether European students should pay the higher university fees paid by other foreigners or be subsidised by UK taxpayers like UK students.

What to know about the US permitting bill, from datacenters to Trump’s arch


Environmental groups are aghast, but supporters say bill might be only chance to speed up clean energy projects




The US Senate has passed a bill to fast-track energy and datacenter projects by removing environmental and legal guardrails. The legislation has caused a fraught divide among Democrats and green groups over whether this will help or hinder the effort to tackle the climate crisis.
The sweeping bill, called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (or Baaja), is now set for passage in the Republican-controlled House of Representatives before being signed by Donald Trump, who has claimed it will boost economic activity and lower energy costs.



What is in the bill?


View image in fullscreen
An oil pipeline in Cushing, Oklahoma. Photograph: Nick Oxford/Bloomberg via Getty Images
Baaja essentially makes it far easier to build things of all descriptions: oil pipelines, power lines, windfarms, datacenters and much more.


It does this by restricting the often lengthy legal challenges to new projects, such as setting a 150-day limit on lawsuits, and weakening the role of key environmental statutes such as the Clean Water Act and the Endangered Species Act in determining the approval of new construction.
Energy-hungry datacenters will get their power more quickly, which in the US is mostly being derived from gas, a planet-heating fossil fuel. Large datacenters will, though, be forced to pay for their own grid and power costs in order to shield nearby communities.
The permitting of new transmission lines, crucial in connecting clean energy to where it is needed, is streamlined with more regional coordination in the process. This element of the bill, which could cut the time to build power lines in half, has been roundly praised by Democrats and green groups.
But the US will essentially be handcuffed to anything approved by the Trump administration, which has sought to throttle clean energy projects while attempting to boost fossil fuel development wherever possible.
Baaja makes it much harder for future administrations and even judges to revoke or amend permits, even if they were issued in a flawed way, and provides companies, including fossil fuel firms, the right to hefty compensation if they can show they were slowed down in some way by the government.

Andy Burnham said the UK will discuss possible options for even closer ties with the EU, after agreeing a deal covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.
The prime minister said it was a "good day" for Britain and Europe, adding the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to £17bn a year. 
European Council President António Costa said the EU remains "open to have the closest possible relationship" with the UK. 
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal "isn't fair" - and Reform's Nigel Farage called it a "betrayal of the British people".
Legislation to implement the deal is expected to be introduced in the UK Parliament next week. 
Burnham arrived in Brussels to finalise the latest stage of the government's post-Brexit "reset" of relations with the EU, which originally began under former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.
The agreements announced on Friday included scrapping most of the checks on British food exports, in return for the UK following some EU regulations, from 2028.
The UK government believes the changes will cut costs for businesses and could bring prices down for shoppers, while critics argue the change will make the UK a "rule taker" from Brussels rather than a rule maker.

The new youth experience scheme will allow up to 100,000 18 to 31 year olds from the EU to travel, work and study in the UK for up to three years. The same number of young Britons will be allowed into Europe. 
The two sides want to ensure that opportunities under the annual scheme will be available to young people by no later than January 2030.
A further six months is available to discuss a deal on tuition fees, which could prove to be a potential stumbling block.
There have been calls from the European side for fees to be reduced for EU students at British universities. The joint statement says any agreement would also be for UK students in the EU.
